Here’s the problem. And this addresses some of the other comments. No, buying/choosing a phone purely based on benchmark scores shouldn’t be the sole reason to skip or pick it. But it can and should be a contributing factor on some level (even if it’s just a little) The other issue is that due to the lower performance, it DEFINITELY impacts gaming on a mobile platform and this is speaking from someone who has both the 9 PXL and the 16 Pro Max. With the lack of performance that could also elude to a lack of efficiency. And in this case, that’s exactly the problem. Does and can any phone heat up or over heat ? Sure! But what does it take to reach those high thermal levels? Since using the 16PM, the phone has only reached very warm temperatures ONCE. With the 9ProXL, it happened very frequently and was guaranteed to happen a couple times a week. Now, I expect, to some degree, that this will be addressed with the switch to TSMC from Samsung architecture. And with that, thermal issues impact battery health and longevity. Internally, Google has a larger battery, by over 300 mAh - but from my day to day usage it lasts nowhere NEAR the 16PM. For example. I can use the Pixel on the same schedule as the iPhone and at around 5pm, my battery on the pixel could be at 20-30%. And the IPhone would still be rocking at 50-60% (sometimes even 70). And this is with similar usage on both phones. I’m not babying the iPhone. In fact I can use the iPhone more and it still wouldn’t drain as fast. So what he’s saying in the video is something I agree with. If you’re not a power user or heavy in to gaming, maybe the pixel will do okay, but even on some basic tasks and what not, Google still hasn’t solved the thermal problem and again - much of that is on Samsung’s table. And I would definitely recommend either the Galaxy or the iPhone. (For the record, for newbs; why would I recommend a Galaxy if Samsung can’t handle the thermals? Because, at least in the states, Samsung uses Qualcomm, not Exynos or other in-house fabrications. And because of that, they don’t experience thermal issues or battery consumption problems to the degree that Pixels currently do. And by the way, I’m not here to bash Pixels. I actually like these phones. But you can’t ignore the realities. In closing - you have to remember that Apple has been integrating custom processors on their iPhones for years and have had their fair share of generation processors that were stove-top sizzlers. Same with Qualcomm and their Snapdragons. But both companies have continued to develop and refine those issues. Google has only been in the game for the past few years and I don’t expect all the problems will go away in the 10th gens, but i do expect to see some sort of improvements with efficiency and thermals.

The reason why IPhone Duo has Apple Pencil support is because Apple used Wacom AES (Active Electro Static) technology, which sends static electric signals to display as input which becomes what you draw and write on thw screen. Samsung on other hand used Wacom EMR (Electromagnetic Resonance) same as Wacom's own digital drawing tablets and stylus. This uses a dgitizer which sends electricity to stylus and an induction coil inside S-Pen converts that into electronic inputs. Result? Battery free design unlike Apple Pencil qhich needs charging after sometime. Drawback is this makes display thicker which made Samsung to abandon the S-Pen after Z Fold 7.

The reason why IPhone Duo has Apple Pencil support is because Apple used Wacom AES (Active Electro Static) technology, which sends static electric signals to display as input which becomes what you draw and write on thw screen. Samsung on other hand used Wacom EMR (Electromagnetic Resonance) same as Wacom's own digital drawing tablets and stylus. This uses a dgitizer which sends electricity to stylus and an induction coil inside S-Pen converts that into electronic inputs. Result? Battery free design unlike Apple Pencil qhich needs charging after sometime. Drawback is this makes display thicker which made Samsung to abandon the S-Pen after Z Fold 7.

I didn’t need all the bells and whistles that I needed when I chose the iPhone 14 Pro Max. I’m a few days into this new phone, and I haven’t found a feature on the base model that I miss that was exclusive to the Pro models. Battery arguments I think that the battery of iPhones is generally very good, and it’s not just about how many mAh the battery has. Samsung has larger batteries for many devices, for example, 5,000 mAh, but a larger battery capacity does not automatically mean that the phone will last longer. Apple is developing its own processor, iOS and energy management very closely together. As a result, the hardware and software are very well coordinated and the power consumption can be controlled efficiently. Especially the A-chips from Apple are very powerful and at the same time energy efficient, so that an iPhone can sometimes achieve a very good runtime with a smaller battery. In addition, iOS manages background processes and apps in a very controlled manner, which means that less energy can be lost in standby. Apple also has the advantage that the company can develop both the hardware and the operating system itself and thus optimise the entire system. Functions such as optimised charging also help to save the battery in the long term. Yes, the iQOO 15 captures slightly better details in HDR, but paying an extra ₹18K just for that makes no sense. The company wants to push the iQOO 15 now, so the iQOO 13 won’t be easily available in the market. But if you can still find the iQOO 13 at a good offline price, that’s the one you should buy. Having read some comments posted here and there, it's becoming increasingly clear to me that some people either didn't have use for or maybe never even perceived the full range of uses for the Bluetooth s-pen. So here's some explanation from a bluetooth s-pen devotee. Some have told us to just use our fingers for navigation, but if that was the only way we liked to navigate we wouldn't be complaining about being limited to it. We PREFER using the s-pen for some things. For example, the s-pen can make it way easier to be precise when selecting text, or to drag and drop, or to create handwriting or visual art. Voice commands to take photos make NOISE, and sometimes we don't want to disturb the people or wildlife around us with noise when we're trying to take a picture. Palm detection isn't always viable or convenient - for example, I've used Bluetooth s-pens to photograph the undercarriages of cars and the back sides of and spaces behind and inside of major appliances for informational purposes where even if I could stick my palm in the space it would be too close for the phone to perceive it. I've used it to photograph my cats and dogs and even camera shy friends and family (who would likely have changed position if I had moved to use a palm gesture or made noise to issue a voice command). I've photographed the tops of things that I can't come close to seeing when I'm standing on the floor but can juuust barely hold my phone high enough to aim the camera at, and while I may not be able to see the shutter button on the phone in those situations, I can hold the s-pen in my other hand and use it to trigger the shutter. Also, using the palm only works with the selfie camera, so if you want to use your main camera the palm is a no-go. Regarding SD cards - it can be much cheaper to buy a one terabyte SD card than it is to upgrade to one terabyte of storage on your phone, and even if your phone becomes irreparably damaged you might be able to rescue the card, and if you manage to fill one card up you can switch it out for another card instead of having to transfer the data from your phone to the cloud (which will be an additional cost) or your laptop or whatever and then delete it from your phone. Not my thing, but I can see how it could be useful to some people. Regarding using the USB port as a headphone jack...I got nothing. I find true wireless Bluetooth headsets much preferable to wired headsets, but maybe I've overlooked something on that issue.

Here’s the problem. And this addresses some of the other comments. No, buying/choosing a phone purely based on benchmark scores shouldn’t be the sole reason to skip or pick it. But it can and should be a contributing factor on some level (even if it’s just a little) The other issue is that due to the lower performance, it DEFINITELY impacts gaming on a mobile platform and this is speaking from someone who has both the 9 PXL and the 16 Pro Max. With the lack of performance that could also elude to a lack of efficiency. And in this case, that’s exactly the problem. Does and can any phone heat up or over heat ? Sure! But what does it take to reach those high thermal levels? Since using the 16PM, the phone has only reached very warm temperatures ONCE. With the 9ProXL, it happened very frequently and was guaranteed to happen a couple times a week. Now, I expect, to some degree, that this will be addressed with the switch to TSMC from Samsung architecture. And with that, thermal issues impact battery health and longevity. Internally, Google has a larger battery, by over 300 mAh - but from my day to day usage it lasts nowhere NEAR the 16PM. For example. I can use the Pixel on the same schedule as the iPhone and at around 5pm, my battery on the pixel could be at 20-30%. And the IPhone would still be rocking at 50-60% (sometimes even 70). And this is with similar usage on both phones. I’m not babying the iPhone. In fact I can use the iPhone more and it still wouldn’t drain as fast. So what he’s saying in the video is something I agree with.
